item.statement: A meth overdose shows up as slow breathing and tiny pupils.
item.why: It's the reverse: it looks like a body in overdrive, with a racing heart, fast breathing, wide pupils and great restlessness. That's second-hand, from two reviews of hospital studies, and how often each sign shows up varies a lot.

lines.short: A meth overdose can look like a body in overdrive. The heart races, breathing speeds up, and people get very restless and upset. Some lose touch with reality.
lines.but: That's second-hand, from two reviews of hospital studies, and how often each sign shows up varies a lot.
how: Signs include a racing heart, high blood pressure, fast breathing and wide pupils. People can be very restless and upset.
The body can get very hot. Chest pain and organ failure can happen, and some people die.
One review found psychosis (losing touch with reality) in 12 to 80 in 100 people seen in hospital. Suicidal thoughts or acts showed up in 6 to 50, depending on the study.
Neither review says how many patients die.

item.statement: The more traditional the ayahuasca ceremony, the less fear people feel.
item.why: In one big survey, more traditional practices went with a little more fear, and church hymns or sermons with less. The differences were small, and people rated everything looking back.

lines.short: Maybe a little. People who felt safer and better supported at their last ceremony recalled a bit less fear. They also reported fewer problems later.
lines.but: One survey: people rated the ceremony and how it went at the same time, looking back.
how: Almost 7,000 people who had drunk ayahuasca answered one online survey about their last ceremony.
Each step up on a 1-to-4 rating of feeling safe and supported went with about 0.3 points less fear, out of 10, and slightly fewer problems in the weeks after.
More traditional practices, and drinking in Amazon countries other than Brazil, went with more fear. Church hymns or sermons went with less.
Fasting showed no link the study could detect with fear or later problems. All the differences were small, and nothing was measured before people drank.

item.statement: Lots of people who take magic mushrooms end up seeking emergency treatment.
item.why: In one big online survey, about 2 in 1,000 people who'd used them in the past year said they had, and nearly all of those felt back to normal within a day. But nobody checked their answers, and anyone who couldn't answer wasn't counted.

lines.short: About 2 in 1,000 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year said they sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After LSD: 10 in 1,000.
lines.but: Volunteers answered an online survey about themselves; nobody checked their answers, and people who could not answer were not counted.
how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 9,233 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year answered this question; 19 said yes.
Of the 19, 13 reported anxiety or panic and 13 paranoia; 8 said they were admitted to hospital.
17 of the 18 who answered felt back to normal within a day, and all within a week.
Those who sought treatment were younger: typically 19, against 23 for the others who answered.

item.statement: One ketamine drip can lift depression within hours.
item.why: A day after one drip, 64 in 100 were much better, against 28 in 100 after a sedative drip. But for most the lift faded within weeks, and people can often tell they got ketamine, which may make it look bigger.

lines.short: It can, within hours. A day after one drip, 64 in 100 were much better, against 28 in 100 after a sedative drip. For most, it faded within weeks.
lines.but: People can often tell they got ketamine, which may make the lift look bigger.
how: In a 2006 trial, 12 of 17 people were much better a day after a ketamine drip. After a salt-water drip, none of 14 were.
In a 2013 trial, 72 people got ketamine or a sedative, picked to make it harder to guess which. Other medicines had failed them.
Pooled trials show the gap is biggest about a day after ketamine. In the 2013 trial, it was not clear by a week.
Two of the 2013 trial's authors were named on patent applications for ketamine in depression. One gave up any share of the money.

item.statement: Teens who remembered more of the US government's anti-drug ads were, if anything, more likely to try cannabis.
item.why: In a national survey, they were no less likely to start, fewer said they definitely wouldn't, and in one of three periods more ads went with more first use. The authors call that tentative, not definitive.

lines.short: No sign they did. Despite nearly $1 billion from Congress, teens' reported cannabis use stayed flat in a national survey, and those who remembered more ads weren't less likely to start.
lines.but: Nearly every teen saw the ads, so there was no group without them to compare cannabis use with.
how: A national survey interviewed 8,117 US kids aged 9 to 18 at home, and many again up to three times, between 1999 and 2004.
94 in 100 remembered seeing anti-drug ads at least monthly. About 24 in 100 teens said they'd ever used cannabis, in 2000 and again in 2004.
Teens who remembered more ads were no less likely to start cannabis by the next interview. Fewer said they definitely wouldn't.
In one of three periods, more ads even went with more first use of cannabis. The authors call this tentative, not definitive.

item.statement: Almost everyone who tries stimulants like meth gets hooked.
item.why: It depends how you count: an old US survey found about 11 in 100 had ever been dependent, and a broader Australian count estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years. Neither had a number for meth alone.

lines.short: It depends how you count. An old US survey found 11 in 100 had ever been dependent; a broader Australian count estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting.
lines.but: Neither survey has a number for meth alone, and the two measured different things, so they can't be compared directly.
how: In the early 1990s, a US survey used set interview questions to find who had ever been dependent on a drug they had used.
Stimulants other than cocaine: about 11 in 100. Tobacco 32, alcohol 15, cocaine 17.
It counted people who had just started, so they had little time to become dependent.
An Australian survey in 2007 counted differently, allowing for when people started. It estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting, but it also counted a related diagnosis called abuse.

item.statement: In UK reports, most people with low blood salt after MDMA had drunk a lot of liquid.
item.why: At least 10 of 17 cases reported to a UK poisons service had, and the 2 who died had brain swelling. These reports count only people who got ill, so they can't show how often it happens or whether drinking more changes the risk.

lines.short: Possibly. Low blood salt (sodium) after MDMA has been reported, mostly in young people; of 17 UK cases, at least 10 had drunk a lot of liquid.
lines.but: These only count people who got ill, so they can't show how often it happens, or whether drinking more changes the risk.
how: Over 28 months, 17 people aged 15 to 26 were reported to a UK poisons service. Of the 15 who survived, 10 had seizures, 12 had a normal temperature at hospital, and 13 recovered fully.
The 2 who died, aged 15 and 18, had brain swelling. Both had drunk a lot of water, and drank or were given more after they began to feel ill.
In California poison-centre records, 73 of 188 people who had their blood salt measured had a low level. 4 of those 73 died.
The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water, so drinking more than it needs waters down the salt. The UK authors say how it happens is not yet known.

item.statement: Weed really is stronger than it used to be, on average.
item.why: Across 7 countries from 1970 to 2017, THC, its main active part, rose about 3 points every 10 years in weed and 6 in hash. But most samples were seized by police, so they may not match what people buy.

lines.short: Yes, on average. In cannabis from 7 countries, 1970 to 2017, THC, its main active part, rose about 3 points every 10 years in weed and 6 in hash.
lines.but: Most samples were cannabis seized by police, not picked at random, so they may not match what people buy.
how: Researchers combined 12 studies from 7 countries that measured THC in cannabis. Most tested police seizures; two Dutch studies bought samples at random in shops.
A point is a share of the weight: 5% to 6% THC is one point. These numbers describe the cannabis, not what people took in.
Not everywhere: US weed rose in every period studied, but weed in the UK (1975–1989) and New Zealand (1979–1996) showed no clear rise.
CBD, another substance in cannabis, did not change. The authors put the weed rise down to stronger kinds selling more, but sales were not measured.

item.statement: On average, people who often use cannabis score a little lower on memory tests.
item.why: A big review found small gaps in learning, memory, attention and planning, but none clear for language, shape or movement. People were tested only after they'd started, so it can't show cannabis caused the gap.

lines.short: On average they score a little lower than people who use little or none.
lines.but: People were tested only after they had started, so the studies can't show that cannabis caused it.
how: A review pooled 69 studies of young people, about 21 years old on average, who used cannabis often.
They scored a little lower on learning, memory, attention and planning tests. Language, shape and movement tests showed no clear gap.
The gap was smaller in studies that asked people to stop for more than 3 days before the test, and bigger in people getting help for their cannabis use. Small studies found bigger gaps.
In a British twin study, the gap at age 18 was no longer clear when each twin was compared with their own twin.

item.statement: The 2002 study claiming ecstasy harmed monkeys' brains had actually given the animals a different drug.
item.why: The drug came from a wrongly labelled bottle, and the study was withdrawn a year later. The withdrawal notice doesn't say what the one animal that got ecstasy showed.

lines.short: A 2002 study said ecstasy harmed monkeys' brains. It was withdrawn a year later.
lines.but: Fewer newspapers told readers about the mistake than told the first story.
how: The animals had been given a different drug, from a wrongly labelled bottle.
Two of the ten animals given the drug died during the study.
Of 50 big US newspapers, 26 wrote about the study and 20 about the withdrawal.
The notice does not say what the one animal that got ecstasy showed.

item.statement: Children adopted away from a birth parent with a drug problem still have drug problems more often.
item.why: In a Swedish study, about 9 in 100 of them had one on record, against 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did. What birth parents pass on includes the pregnancy, not just genes.

lines.short: Both are linked: what comes from birth parents, and the home a child grows up in.
lines.but: One Swedish study. What birth parents pass on includes the pregnancy, not just genes.
how: In Sweden, 18,115 adopted children born 1950 to 1993 were followed in health, prescription and court records until 2009.
Some birth parents had a drug problem on record. Their children, raised by adoptive parents, had one about twice as often: about 9 in 100, against 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did.
Adoptive brothers and sisters are not related by birth. Still, 6 in 100 of them had a drug problem when the adopted child had one, against 3 in 100 when the child did not.

The study did not work out a share due to genes. Where studies give one, it is about differences between people in one place and time. It does not say how much of your own risk comes from genes, and it can change when living conditions change.

item.statement: In most published 'excited delirium' deaths, force such as restraint was recorded.
item.why: Force, including sedation and electrical weapons as well as restraint, was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths among published cases. These were selected reports, so they can't tell how much restraint, drugs or the agitated state caused a death.

lines.short: The label alone does not establish what caused a death.
lines.but: The cases were selected for reports. They cannot give the risk per encounter.
how: The reviews describe extreme agitation, but no validated definition or specific autopsy sign. The label is also used with living people.
In 168 published cases, force was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths. That included sedation and electrical weapons as well as physical restraint.
Only 3 cases explicitly had no force; 28 had missing information. A later review also cites deaths attributed to the label without overt restraint.
Researchers disagree about restraint, drugs and the agitated state. These reports cannot tell how much each caused.

item.statement: In one US survey, about 14 in 100 adults had alcohol use disorder in the past year.
item.why: Two or more of 11 signs of problem drinking in a year count, and about half the cases were mild. Another US survey found a little over half as many, so the number depends on the survey.

lines.short: In a US survey, 14 in 100 adults had it in the past year.
lines.but: Another US survey found a little over half as many, so the number depends on the survey.
how: Alcohol use disorder is found with a list of 11 signs of problem drinking: 2 or more in a year count. In 2012 and 2013, a US survey asked 36,309 adults set questions to find it.
About 14 in 100 adults had it in the past year, and 29 in 100 at some time in their lives. About half of the past-year cases were mild. It was most common at ages 18 to 29: about 27 in 100.
The survey's authors think it became more common after 2001. We think their two surveys were run too differently to show that.
The survey missed people who were homeless or in prison, and most people in treatment. For the world, a review passes on an estimate of about 5 in 100 people aged 15 or older.

item.statement: Caffeine doesn't really change how much you sleep that night.
item.why: Across 24 studies comparing nights with and without caffeine in the same people, they slept about 45 minutes less after caffeine, and their sleep was lighter. These were healthy adults with low to moderate usual intake, so heavy users, teenagers and older adults may differ.

lines.short: After caffeine, people slept about 45 minutes less than on nights without caffeine.
lines.but: The people studied were healthy adults with low to moderate usual caffeine intake, so heavy users, teenagers and older adults may differ.
how: 24 studies compared nights after caffeine with nights without it, in the same people.
Caffeine made falling asleep slower, time awake in the night longer, and sleep lighter.
The more caffeine, and the closer to bedtime, the more sleep people lost.
In five studies, people did not report more time awake in the night.

item.statement: In small trials, cannabis medicines controlled sickness from chemotherapy better than a dummy did.
item.why: About 47 in 100 on a cannabis medicine had their sickness fully controlled, against 20 in 100 on a dummy. But only 102 people were in these three trials, and most trials in the review had serious weaknesses.

lines.short: In three small trials, more people had their sickness fully controlled than with a dummy.
lines.but: Only 102 people were in these three trials, and most trials had weaknesses.
how: Researchers combined three trials. People having chemotherapy got a cannabis medicine or a dummy medicine (placebo).
About 47 in 100 people on the medicine had their sickness fully controlled, against 20 in 100 on the dummy.
Most other trials compared cannabis medicines with other sickness medicines. The review says these leaned towards cannabis too. But it did not combine them.
23 of the 28 trials had serious weaknesses in how they were run or reported.

item.statement: Making fentanyl test strips legal has been shown to cut drug deaths.
item.why: After the laws, deaths ran about 7 in 100 below the expected trend, but the study didn't check whether more people used strips, and the drop came in each law's very first month. Other changes at the same time could explain it.

lines.short: After the law, drug deaths ran about 3 a year per 100,000 people below other states' trend.
lines.but: It looked at laws, not at people using strips. Other changes at the same time could explain it.
how: Researchers used death records from every US state from 2018 to 2022. They counted 15 states and Washington, DC as making the strips legal in that time.

After the law, there were about 3 fewer drug deaths a year for every 100,000 people, about 7 in 100 fewer than expected. Once age, rural living and income were allowed for, this was about the same for White and Black people, though less certain for Black people.
The study did not check whether more people got or used strips. It counted deaths from any drug, and the drop came in the very first month of each law.

The researchers chose the law dates themselves. They kept Alabama, Minnesota and New Mexico among the states without a law, though laws started there in 2021 and 2022, and moved two other dates later. They showed no results with their source's dates.

item.statement: Passing out from GHB again and again has been linked to worse memory.
item.why: In one Dutch study, people who had passed out many times remembered worse than people who used GHB regularly without passing out, and than people who used other drugs. It can't show GHB caused it, and nobody checked whether memory improves.

lines.short: GHB affects memory while it works; in one study, people who had passed out from GHB many times had worse memory than other people who used GHB or other drugs.
lines.but: That one Dutch study cannot show GHB caused the memory problems, and nobody checked if they improve.
how: Lab studies found that GHB affects memory and coordination while it is working.
The review says it is not yet known whether these short-term memory effects fully wear off.
One study found that people who had passed out from GHB many times had worse memory than people who used GHB regularly without passing out, and than people who used other drugs but never GHB.

item.statement: Ketamine drips for depression cause memory loss as often as ECT does.
item.why: In a Swedish trial, 19 of 90 had memory loss lasting over a day after ECT, against none of 91 after ketamine drips. Everyone knew which treatment they got.

lines.short: Two big trials disagree: a US trial found ketamine drips at least as good as ECT. But in Swedish hospital patients, 63 in 100 got well on ECT, against 46.
lines.but: Everyone knew whether they got ketamine or ECT, and the trials took different people, so nobody knows why they disagree.
how: In a US trial of 403 adults, mostly outpatients without psychosis, 55 in 100 on ketamine drips said their depression halved, against 41 on ECT.
In a Swedish trial of 186 hospital patients, some with psychosis, 63 in 100 got well after ECT, against 46 after ketamine.
A review combining hospital trials also found ECT eased depression more than ketamine, but about half its data came from that Swedish trial.
In Sweden, 19 of 90 had memory loss lasting over a day after ECT, against none of 91 after ketamine drips.

item.statement: People who use ecstasy score worse on memory tests even if they use hardly any other drug.
item.why: In one study where breath, urine and hair tests checked that people used little else, memory scores didn't differ from others in the same all-night dance scene. Medium-sized differences couldn't be ruled out, and heavier use went with worse scores on one planning test.

lines.short: In people who used ecstasy but hardly any other drug, memory scores were no different.
lines.but: It was one study, and medium-sized differences could not be ruled out.
how: 52 people who used ecstasy were compared with 59 people from the same all-night dance scene.
Breath, urine and hair tests checked that they had used little else.
Memory scores did not differ, and most of the 40 measures were similar.
People who had used it more than 50 times did worse on one planning test.

item.statement: Parkinson's disease is common in people diagnosed with meth or amphetamine problems.
item.why: In Utah health records of people with such diagnoses and no other drug or alcohol diagnosis, it was diagnosed about 3 times as often, but that's about 3 in 1,000 over about 7 years, against 1 in 1,000. Some diagnoses were probably other movement conditions.

lines.short: Parkinson's was diagnosed more often in people with a meth or amphetamine diagnosis and no other drug or alcohol diagnosis.
lines.but: It stays rare: about 3 in 1,000 over about 7 years. Some diagnoses are probably other conditions, and medicine side effects were not ruled out.
how: In Utah health records, Parkinson's was diagnosed about 3 times as often in people with meth or amphetamine diagnoses and no other drug or alcohol diagnoses.
That is about 3 in 1,000 against 1 in 1,000, over about 7 years.
A California study found a smaller increase.
The records probably include other movement conditions.

item.statement: In most recent US overdose deaths involving meth, meth was the only drug.
item.why: Medical examiners' reports from 2021 to mid-2024 found fentanyl or other opioids in about 7 in 10 of these deaths. That's a different kind of record from the yearly death counts.

lines.short: In the US, meth use rose from 2015 to 2019, and deaths involving meth kept rising through 2023, the latest year counted.
lines.but: Many of these deaths also involved fentanyl or other opioids. The rise slowed after 2021.
how: In US surveys, past-year meth use rose by about a fifth from 2015 to 2019.
Deaths involving meth rose from about 550 in 1999 to about 35,000 in 2023. The rise slowed after 2021.
Medical examiners' reports from 2021 to mid-2024: about 7 in 10 overdose deaths involving meth also involved opioids. This is a different kind of record from the death counts.
The surveys miss people who are homeless or living in places like prisons and hospitals.

item.statement: The link between cannabis and car crashes stays just as strong when studies allow for drinking.
item.why: It shrinks: studies that allowed for alcohol found about 1.1 to 1.2 times the odds of a crash, against 1.7 to 1.8 in studies that didn't. These compare crashed drivers with others, so they can't show one driver's chance of crashing.

lines.short: Drivers with cannabis in a test were linked to more crashes.
lines.but: These studies compare crashed drivers with others, so they cannot show one driver's chance of crashing.
how: Across 28 results from 21 studies in 13 countries, drivers with cannabis found in a test had about 1.2 to 1.4 times the odds of a crash, or of being at fault in one.
An older review found 1.9 times. Re-checking its counts and allowing for other factors brought the same studies to between 1.2 and 1.4.
Studies that allowed for alcohol found 1.1 to 1.2 times. Studies that did not found 1.7 to 1.8 times.
A positive test shows cannabis was in the body, not that a driver was impaired.

item.statement: People on methadone become fully tolerant to its effect on breathing.
item.why: In two studies of people on methadone, tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete. Reviews add that tolerance may drop during a break from opioids, so the usual amount may hit much harder, breathing included.

lines.short: Tolerance may drop during a break from opioids, two reviews say. So the usual amount may hit much harder, breathing included.
lines.but: The reviews give no numbers. Not how long a break must be, or how much the risk of a fatal overdose rises.
how: The older review offers this as a possible explanation. It says tolerance may fade quickly, and not at the same pace for every effect. But there's little data on how fast.
The idea rests on one hair study. People who died of heroin overdose had less morphine in their hair than people still using. The review reads that as less use before death.
The newer review gives prison and detox as examples of a break; the older one, which it cites, doesn't.
Two studies of people on methadone found tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete.

item.statement: Music has been shown to make ketamine treatment for depression work better.
item.why: Nobody knows yet whether it changes how well ketamine works. In a trial of 32 patients, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less with music, and the report gave no results on how sessions felt.

lines.short: Nobody knows yet whether it changes how a session feels or how well ketamine works. One trial found the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less with music.
lines.but: Just 32 patients; the report gave no results on how the sessions felt.
how: 32 patients with hard-to-treat depression were starting a course of six ketamine drips. Chance decided who heard music during each drip; the rest heard none.
With music, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less during each drip. The bottom number didn't clearly differ.
Before that, a review found 14 studies of music with ketamine. In most, ketamine came with other drugs during medical procedures. None compared music with no music in treating depression.
The review's case reports and interviews had no comparison. Some said music eased the detached feeling or blocked distractions; others heard it warped, or felt it kept them tied to the outside world.

item.statement: Bad trips are fairly common among people who've used psychedelics.
item.why: 41 in 100 people who'd used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip, and 5 in 100 said one had badly affected their daily life. That's one online survey of US adults looking back over their whole lives.

lines.short: Fairly common: 41 in 100 people who'd used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip. 5 in 100 said one had badly affected their daily life.
lines.but: That's one online survey, and people were looking back over their whole lives.
how: 613 US adults who had ever used a psychedelic answered one online survey in 2021, looking back over their whole life.
Most were glad they had used psychedelics: 79 in 100 agreed, at least a little.
In the days or weeks after their hardest trip, 7 in 100 said they'd thought of hurting themselves or others, or tried to.

57 in 100 said a problem like worry or poor sleep lasted at least a few days, and put it down to psychedelics. But people who hadn't used them weren't asked, so it's unknown how many would have had these anyway.

item.statement: Psilocybin has been shown to help people quit smoking.
item.why: In one small study, 12 of just 15 people given psilocybin plus lots of counselling weren't smoking 6 months later. With no comparison group, no one can tell what psilocybin added.

lines.short: Not known. In one small study, 12 of 15 people given psilocybin plus lots of counselling weren't smoking 6 months later.
lines.but: There was no comparison group, so no one can tell what psilocybin added to all the counselling.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 15 adults who had smoked for 31 years on average got 15 weeks of counselling and psilocybin two or three times.
Six months on, breath and urine tests confirmed 12 of 15 given psilocybin weren't smoking. Four of those 12 had smoked again at some point.
The psilocybin paper cites 45 to 59 in 100 not smoking after intensive standard treatment. With so few people, 12 of 15 isn't clearly better.

item.statement: A US survey found tobacco hooked a bigger share of people who'd used it than cocaine or meth-like stimulants.
item.why: Tobacco 32 in 100, cocaine 17, stimulants other than cocaine about 11, in an early-1990s survey that included people who'd only just started. A broader Australian count, done differently, estimated about 50 in 100 for stimulants within 14 years of starting.

lines.short: It depends how you count. An old US survey found 11 in 100 had ever been dependent; a broader Australian count estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting.
lines.but: Neither survey has a number for meth alone, and the two measured different things, so they can't be compared directly.
how: In the early 1990s, a US survey used set interview questions to find who had ever been dependent on a drug they had used.
Stimulants other than cocaine: about 11 in 100. Tobacco 32, alcohol 15, cocaine 17.
It counted people who had just started, so they had little time to become dependent.
An Australian survey in 2007 counted differently, allowing for when people started. It estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting, but it also counted a related diagnosis called abuse.

item.statement: In one study, daily use of strong cannabis went with about 5 times the odds of psychosis.
item.why: That's compared with never using, in 11 places in Europe and Brazil. Daily use of weaker types went with about 2 times, and the gap between strong and weaker could be chance.

lines.short: Daily use of strong types had the strongest link with psychosis, but the gap from weaker types could be chance.
lines.but: Strength was guessed from the type people named, and both studies come from one team.
how: Two studies by one team, one in south London and one in 11 places in Europe and Brazil, compared people who had a first psychosis with people from the same areas who had not.

In 11 places in Europe and Brazil, daily use of strong types (10% THC or more on average) went with about 5 times the odds of psychosis, compared with never using. Daily use of weaker types went with about 2 times; the gap between the two could be chance.

In the 11 places, using any type only now and then was not linked to psychosis. In London, using strong types less than once a week went with nearly 2 times the odds, but some numbers in that study do not add up. In both studies, weaker types were not linked once all patterns of use were counted together.
Nobody tested the cannabis: people named the type they had used after they became ill, and its strength was taken from police, European and national figures.

item.statement: Teens who use the most cannabis report suicidal thoughts and attempts more often than teens who don't.
item.why: A review of three studies each found about 1.5 times the odds of suicidal thoughts and 3.5 times the odds of attempts in teens who used the most. That can't show cause: in other studies, the link shrank or went away once depression, alcohol and hard living conditions were counted.

lines.short: Teens who used cannabis the most reported suicidal thoughts or attempts more often than teens who didn't.
lines.but: Only three studies each, mostly measured in the teen years; they cannot show cause.
how: A review combined three long-term studies on suicidal thoughts and three on suicide attempts.
Teens in the highest-use group had about 1.5 times the odds of suicidal thoughts and about 3.5 times the odds of attempts, compared with teens who did not use cannabis.
In two of the three studies for each, this was measured while the young people were still teenagers.
In other studies, the link shrank or went away once depression, alcohol and hard living conditions were taken into account.

item.statement: Muscle jerks and shaking are key signs doctors look for in serotonin syndrome.
item.why: Doctors check for muscle jerks, shaking with very brisk reflexes, sweating and restlessness, and in severe cases stiff muscles with a high fever. A checklist of these signs was tested in one hospital unit, on overdoses.

lines.short: Doctors look for muscle jerks, shaking, sweating and restlessness when serotonin may be too high.
lines.but: The checklist was tested in one hospital unit, on overdoses, against that unit's own diagnosis.
how: Serotonin toxicity (also called serotonin syndrome) is too much serotonin activity, caused by drugs that raise serotonin. It ranges from mild to severe.
Doctors examine the person for muscle jerks, shaking with very brisk reflexes, and, when severe, stiff muscles with a high fever.
In one Australian hospital unit, a checklist of these signs matched the unit's diagnosis in about 84 of 100 people diagnosed. An older checklist matched about 75 of 100.
Everyone had taken an overdose, and mild signs can look like ordinary drug effects. No independent test of the checklist was found.

item.statement: The day after some benzo sleeping pills, people drove worse than with alcohol at a common drink-driving limit.
item.why: In tests in a real car or a driving machine, weaving inside the lane was worse with some pills than with alcohol at the limit used in several countries. Most studies tested one night in healthy volunteers, not people who take these pills for months.

lines.short: Some benzodiazepine sleeping pills made people drive worse the next day than after dummy pills.
lines.but: Most studies tested one night in healthy volunteers, not people who take these pills for months.
how: Volunteers drove a real car or a driving machine the day after a pill or a dummy pill.
Researchers measured how much the car weaved inside its lane.
With some pills the weaving was worse than with alcohol at the driving limit used in several countries.
With other pills or lower doses, weaving was not clearly different from dummy pills, but each result came from one small study.

item.statement: People with no working version of the enzyme that clears MDMA get far higher levels of it.
item.why: Their peak level was only about 15 percent higher, and only in the first 3 hours: MDMA seems to switch that enzyme off itself, so these body differences matter less. Just 7 such people were studied.

lines.short: MDMA seems to switch off the enzyme that clears it, so body differences matter less.
lines.but: Only 7 people had no working enzyme, and no study gave a second dose of MDMA.
how: Among 139 volunteers in eight lab studies, the 7 with no working CYP2D6 had a peak MDMA level about 15 percent higher, in the first 3 hours only.
In 15 men, tests after one MDMA dose looked like those of people with no working enzyme in 10 of them. The enzyme had not fully recovered after 10 days.
Medicines that block the enzyme raised the MDMA peak by about 15 to 20 percent. Paroxetine raised it by 16 percent in 12 men.
Bodies that differ are one reason a person can feel little from an amount and take more. None of these studies gave a second dose, so what happens then is not known.

item.statement: Rat Park has been repeated, with the same result.
item.why: Two later experiments meant to repeat the 1981 Rat Park morphine study did not find the same result. In the original studies, the two groups also drank from different machines, measured differently, and all of it was in rats.

lines.short: Less than is often said. Rats living together drank less morphine water, but only in some tests.
lines.but: All of this was in rats, so it says nothing direct about people.
how: In 1979, by the last test, rats kept alone drank 5 to over 16 times as much sweet morphine water as rats living together.
In 1978, when morphine water was almost all they had to drink, the rats living together drank more of it.
In all three studies, the two groups drank morphine water from different machines, measured differently. That could explain part of the gap.
Two later experiments meant to repeat the 1981 Rat Park morphine study did not find the same result.

item.statement: In a UK scan study, 35 in 100 people who barely drank had a memory area rated 'shrunken'.
item.why: 'Shrunken' meant doctors saw any sign of shrinkage at all. People who drank more got the rating more often, but the study can't show alcohol caused it.

lines.short: In one UK study, people who drank more alcohol more often had a memory area rated 'shrunken' on a scan. So did 35 in 100 who barely drank.
lines.but: Each brain was scanned once, so the study shows a link, not shrinking, and not that alcohol caused it.
how: 527 UK government workers, mostly men, reported how much alcohol they drank over 30 years, then had one brain scan around age 70.
'Shrunken' meant doctors saw any sign of shrinkage at all. Even 35 in 100 people who barely drank alcohol got that rating.
The paper's 'three times the odds' came from the top of its 'moderate' range for men; lower down, the study was too small to tell.
Only one of three thinking tests (naming words that start with a letter) fell slightly faster with more drinking. No test at the scan differed.

item.statement: Most people treated in hospital for alcohol withdrawal get the DTs (sudden confusion).
item.why: A review says 3 to 5 in 100 of them do, and that about 1 to 4 in 100 hospital patients with the DTs die. Most of these figures are passed on by that review or come from old trials.

lines.short: Sudden confusion in alcohol withdrawal; a few in 100 people in hospital get it.
lines.but: Most figures are passed on by one review or come from old trials, mostly one from 1969.
how: The DTs are confusion that comes on fast and comes and goes, together with signs of withdrawal such as shaking or a fast pulse.
A review says the DTs usually start about 3 days after withdrawal begins and last 2 or 3 days. It says 3 to 5 in 100 people in hospital for withdrawal get them.
In old trials, about 6 in 100 people in withdrawal who got dummy pills developed delirium. Most of these people were in one trial from 1969.
The review says about 1 to 4 in 100 hospital patients with the DTs die. It names recent seizures, earlier DTs, older age and other illnesses as signs they are more likely.

item.statement: Most people in treatment for cocaine say they've had paranoia or similar symptoms with it.
item.why: In a review of 17 studies, 68 in 100 said so, while strict diagnostic interviews found a psychotic disorder in 16 in 100. Many also used alcohol or other drugs, so the review can't show cocaine alone caused it.

lines.short: 68 in 100 people treated for cocaine reported psychotic symptoms; 16 in 100 had a diagnosed disorder.
lines.but: These were people in treatment, and many also used alcohol or other drugs.
how: One review pooled 17 studies of 5,286 people, mostly in treatment for cocaine in the US and Spain.
Asked about symptoms such as paranoia, 68 in 100 said they had had them with cocaine. Strict diagnostic interviews found a psychotic disorder in 16 in 100.
The review could not separate cocaine from the alcohol and other drugs people used, so it cannot show cocaine alone caused it.
Other studies the review cites say the symptoms usually pass after stopping, but can get worse with more use and last for weeks.

item.statement: In one study, more babies exposed to ecstasy in pregnancy had birth defects than expected.
item.why: 12 of 78 babies born alive, about 15 in 100, had a birth defect, against the 2 to 3 in 100 the authors expected. But there was no comparison group, almost half the enquiries were lost to follow-up, and many pregnancies also involved other drugs.

lines.short: One study counted birth defects after ecstasy in pregnancy, but it cannot show cause.
lines.but: There was no comparison group, and almost half of the enquiries were lost to follow-up.
how: A UK information service followed 136 pregnancies in which ecstasy was used, nearly all in the first 3 months. 62 of them also involved other drugs.
Of 78 babies born alive, 12 (about 15 in 100) had a birth defect, a mix of minor and major ones. The authors expected 2 to 3 in 100.
Two babies had heart defects and three had a twisted foot. The authors say the study is too small to confirm a link with any one defect.

A later study followed babies of 28 women who used ecstasy but did not report a count of birth defects. One baby had a rare genetic condition, which the authors say cannot be tied to the mother's drug use.

item.statement: In the largest trial, drug tests confirmed the antidepressant mirtazapine cut meth use.
item.why: People on mirtazapine said they used meth about 2 fewer days in 4 weeks than people on a dummy pill, but saliva drug tests showed no difference, and most kept using. Two small San Francisco trials did find fewer meth-positive urine tests.

lines.short: In three trials, people on a depression medicine, mirtazapine, used somewhat less meth than on a dummy pill.
lines.but: Most people kept using, and in the largest trial drug tests showed no difference.
how: Two small San Francisco trials, in men who have sex with men who also had counselling, found fewer meth-positive urine tests on mirtazapine.
A larger Australian trial: people said they cut down by about 2 more days in 4 weeks.
Its saliva drug tests showed no difference, and most people kept using.
Drowsiness was more common on mirtazapine.

item.statement: US deaths involving meth were still rising in 2023.
item.why: They went from about 550 in 1999 to about 35,000 in 2023, though the rise slowed after 2021. Many of these deaths also involved fentanyl or other opioids.

lines.short: In the US, meth use rose from 2015 to 2019, and deaths involving meth kept rising through 2023, the latest year counted.
lines.but: Many of these deaths also involved fentanyl or other opioids. The rise slowed after 2021.
how: In US surveys, past-year meth use rose by about a fifth from 2015 to 2019.
Deaths involving meth rose from about 550 in 1999 to about 35,000 in 2023. The rise slowed after 2021.
Medical examiners' reports from 2021 to mid-2024: about 7 in 10 overdose deaths involving meth also involved opioids. This is a different kind of record from the death counts.
The surveys miss people who are homeless or living in places like prisons and hospitals.

item.statement: The grumpiness and restlessness of quitting smoking usually last for months.
item.why: Most of these feelings were strongest in the first week and gone within 2 to 4 weeks, though for some people they lasted longer or came back. That comes from one expert's summary of older studies.

lines.short: After stopping smoking, people can feel grumpy, anxious and restless, and wake more at night, for weeks.
lines.but: This comes from one expert's summary of older studies; it does not say how many people get each feeling.
how: The studies asked the same people how they felt before and after they stopped smoking.
Most of these feelings were strongest in the first week and gone within 2 to 4 weeks.
Feeling tired, headaches and sweating did not go up after stopping.
For some people the feelings lasted longer or came back after about three weeks.

item.statement: A bad reaction to PCP always wears off within about a day.
item.why: In three cases reported in 1975, a severe breakdown after drugs thought to contain PCP lasted two to four weeks, then passed. Only three cases, and nobody tested the drugs they'd taken.

lines.short: In three reported cases, a severe breakdown lasted two to four weeks, then passed.
lines.but: Only three cases from 1975, and nobody tested the drugs they had taken.
how: Three young men were treated in one hospital after street drugs thought to contain PCP.
They were confused, angry and unsteady, two heard voices, and one jumped from a high window.
All three got better, and afterwards remembered little of their illness.
Earlier studies the doctors cited said the mind effects of PCP usually last about a day.

item.statement: Few people who go to harm reduction sites use drugs alone.
item.why: In a survey at 27 sites in British Columbia, about 3 in 4 had used alone at least once in the past week, most often because it was easier and more comfortable at home. It's one survey, of people already going to these sites.

lines.short: Very common: 76 in 100 people at harm reduction sites said they'd used alone at least once in the past week. The most-picked reason: it's easier and more comfortable at home.
lines.but: It's one survey in one part of Canada, of people who already went to these sites.
how: In 2018, 414 people at 27 sites in British Columbia, Canada, answered a survey. The sites hand out safer-use supplies.
Of those who used alone, 44 in 100 said using at home was easier and more comfortable; 14 in 100 did not want others to know. Some wrote that they had no one to use with.
People who used alone more often had no steady home: 38 in 100, against 24 in 100 of those who didn't.
The survey could not show if using alone changes overdose risk. It cites coroners' reports. They found that about 7 in 10 people who died of an overdose there in 2016 and 2017 were using alone.

item.statement: In one big survey, people sought emergency treatment more often after LSD than after magic mushrooms.
item.why: About 10 in 1,000 people who'd used LSD in the past year said they had, mostly for panic, anxiety or confusion, against 2 in 1,000 after magic mushrooms. Nobody checked the answers, or whether the drug was really LSD.

lines.short: About 10 in 1,000 people who'd used LSD in the past year, and answered, said they'd sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After magic mushrooms: 2 in 1,000.
lines.but: Volunteers took an online survey about themselves. Nobody checked their answers, or if the drug was really LSD.
how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 10,293 people who had used LSD in the past year answered this question; 102 said yes.
Most of the 102 ticked panic, anxiety or confusion. 21 ticked thoughts or acts of self-harm. About half said they were admitted to hospital.
Of about 98 who said how long it lasted, 58 felt back to normal within a day, 40 took longer, and 11 still had problems after 4 weeks.
People with a past mental health diagnosis reported seeking emergency treatment more often: 1.8 in 100, against 0.7 in 100.

item.statement: In a UK study, readers judged a man who died from drugs more harshly than a woman.
item.why: With story details picked at random, readers were also harsher when the story said heroin rather than ecstasy, or an older person with years of use. The differences were small to moderate, and readers answered straight after one made-up story.

lines.short: Yes, somewhat. Readers judged the person who died more harshly when the story said heroin, not ecstasy, or an older person with years of use.
lines.but: Readers saw one made-up story and answered straight away; nobody checked what they did later.
how: In 2022, 1,248 adults in the UK each read one made-up news story about a drug death, with the details chosen at random.
Readers judged the person more harshly when the person was a man, was older and had used the drug for years, or had taken heroin rather than ecstasy. The differences were small to moderate.
Support for services that reduce harm, such as drug checking, barely changed.
The study could not tell the effect of age apart from the effect of using the drug for longer.

item.statement: MDMA only raises body temperature when people dance in hot, crowded places.
item.why: Even resting in a room at about 23 degrees, 24 in 100 lab volunteers went over 38 degrees after MDMA, against 9 in 100 after a dummy pill. Heat, dancing and crowds weren't tested.

lines.short: One dose pushes all three up. In lab tests, 24 in 100 people went over 38 degrees after MDMA, against 9 in 100 after a dummy pill.
lines.but: Healthy volunteers rested in a room at about 23 degrees. Heat, dancing, crowds, other drugs and extra doses weren't tested.
how: 136 healthy adults got one lab dose. The top blood-pressure number went above 160 in 38 in 100 after MDMA, against 6 in 100 after a dummy pill.
A heart rate above 100 happened in 33 in 100 after MDMA, against 2 in 100 after the dummy pill.
Ear temperature went above 38 degrees in 24 in 100 after MDMA, against 9 in 100; the highest was 39.1 degrees.
Four people felt no effect and the study does not say what their bodies did. Everyone got a set dose, so taking more was not tested here.

item.statement: People who had their first drink at 14 or younger more often had alcohol dependence than late starters.
item.why: In a big US survey, about 4 to 5 in 10 who started at 14 or younger had been dependent at some time, against 8 in 100 who started at 25 or older. But people had to remember their first drink, and some of the link seems to come from things that lead to both.

lines.short: Not known. Some of the link seems to come from things that lead to both.
lines.but: Only a few small studies followed young people over time; the big survey relied on memory.
how: In a big US survey in 1992, about 4 to 5 in 10 adults who started drinking at 14 or younger had been dependent on alcohol at some time, against 8 in 100 who started at 25 or older. They had to remember their first drink.
A review found only four groups of young people whose first drink was recorded as teenagers and who were followed into adulthood.
Drinking early went with more drinking problems in some of them. In others the link went away once other risks, such as behaviour problems, were taken into account.

In US twins, the twin who drank without permission by about 15 drank more as an adult than the other twin, even in identical twins. But in identical twins it was not clearly linked to signs of an alcohol disorder.

item.statement: The serotonin changes seen on scans of people who used ecstasy are known to be permanent.
item.why: Nobody knows: three studies found more of the scan marker in people who had stopped longer ago, two found no link with time, and no one has been scanned while using and again years later.

lines.short: We do not know if the marker goes back to normal after people stop.
lines.but: Nobody has been scanned while using and then again years later.
how: Three studies compared different people and found more marker in those who stopped longer ago.
Two other studies found no link with time since the last pill.
People who stop may be different from people who keep going.
The parts that looked normal again are not where the drop is biggest.

item.statement: Reviews rank MDMA with an MAOI antidepressant, like moclobemide, as the riskiest mix they list.
item.why: Four young people in Finland died with MDMA and moclobemide in their blood, and pathologists called each death an accidental poisoning with the two drugs. Four deaths can't give a rate, and all four also had other drugs.

lines.short: Four young people in Finland died with MDMA and moclobemide, an antidepressant, in their blood.
lines.but: Four deaths cannot give a rate, and all four also had other drugs in their blood or urine.
how: None of the four had been prescribed moclobemide. Pathologists called each death an accidental poisoning with the two drugs.
The authors thought it was serotonin syndrome, but its defining signs were not recorded. MDMA levels were about 5 to 6 times the top of the range the paper quotes.
Reviews rank MDMA with this kind of antidepressant as the highest-risk mix they list. Nobody has counted people who took both and had no such outcome.
Some people feel little from an amount of MDMA and take more. No study measured what happens then with this antidepressant.

item.statement: People describe the crash after a cocaine binge as very low mood, then long, heavy sleep.
item.why: Thirty people who sought help for heavy cocaine use also described hunger, and some had passing thoughts of suicide that stayed within the crash. It's what people in treatment told their doctors, so it can't show how often this happens.

lines.short: After a binge, people described a crash: very low mood, then long, heavy sleep and hunger.
lines.but: This is what some people in treatment told their doctors; it cannot show how often it happens.
how: Doctors talked with 30 people who came for help with heavy cocaine use; there was no comparison group.
The crash began soon after the last use and usually ended within a few days.
Some people had passing thoughts of suicide, which were limited to the crash.
Many had used alcohol or other drugs to get to sleep.

item.statement: In trials, a CBD medicine at least halved seizures for most children with Dravet syndrome, a severe childhood epilepsy.
item.why: It did for 43 to 49 in 100 children, against 26 to 27 in 100 on a dummy liquid. The maker ran both trials, and in its own backup checks the result didn't always hold up.

lines.short: In two trials, a CBD medicine cut seizures in Dravet syndrome. Seizures at least halved in 43 to 49 in 100 children, against 26 to 27 on a dummy liquid.
lines.but: The maker ran both trials, and in its own backup checks the result did not always hold up.
how: First trial, 120 children: seizures at least halved in 43 in 100 on CBD and 27 on the dummy liquid. That gap could be chance.
Second trial, 198 children: 44 and 49 in 100 in two CBD groups saw seizures at least halve. On the dummy liquid, 26 did.
The second report said backup checks agreed. Yet with missing diary days filled in, one CBD group no longer clearly beat the dummy liquid.
On CBD, 23 to 36 in 100 children were sleepy, against 10 to 14 on the dummy liquid. Shop CBD was not tested.

item.statement: In sleep labs, people who stopped heavy cannabis use got more dream sleep in the first nights.
item.why: They also slept less and took longer to fall asleep in the first week after stopping. That's from three small studies, two of them from the 1970s, so how long it lasts isn't known.

lines.short: Sleep got shorter and slower to start, with more dream sleep, in the first nights.
lines.but: Three small studies, two of them from the 1970s with very strong lab doses.
how: Sleep was measured in a lab while people were still using cannabis and after they stopped.
After stopping, they slept less, took longer to fall asleep and had more dream (REM) sleep.
The pooled data came from the first week after stopping, so this review cannot say how long the changes last.

item.statement: Fentanyl test strips can miss some drugs related to fentanyl, like carfentanil.
item.why: In lab tests of 28 related drugs on four brands, three never showed up on any brand, and carfentanil showed only at high amounts. These were mostly pure drugs in water, tested by lab staff.

lines.short: In lab tests, strips found most related drugs, but not all. Carfentanil needed large amounts.
lines.but: These were mostly pure drugs in water, tested by lab staff. The largest study reported no repeat tests.
how: One lab tested 28 related drugs on four brands. At high amounts, 21 to 24 of them showed up.
At lower amounts, only 5 to 12 of the 23 tested showed up.
Three never showed up on any brand. Carfentanil showed only at high amounts, and never on one brand.
A second lab found 11 of 13 related drugs on all five batches of one brand. On two of the three newer batches, carfentanil showed only in very large amounts.

item.statement: In small MDMA trials, tiredness was common in the week after a session.
item.why: Five small trials gave MDMA to 58 people with conditions like anxiety or depression; a tight jaw, thirst and sweating were common during sessions, and none of the side effects were serious. The trials were too small to show rare or later harms.

lines.short: In small trials, MDMA's side effects were common and brief, and none were serious.
lines.but: These trials were too small to show rare or later harms.
how: Five small studies gave MDMA to 58 people. They had anxiety, depression, social anxiety with autism, or PTSD in couples.
A tight jaw, thirst, sweating and headache were common during sessions. Tiredness was common in the week after.
Blood pressure, pulse and body heat went up during sessions. None of this needed treatment.
Thoughts of suicide were recorded as side effects in a few people; in one trial this was as common with the dummy pill.
